slides.title: Internal and inter-laboratory quality control and its characteristics
bullets: Organization of laboratory services. Medical ethics and deontology
Practical session — 4 h
Lecture — 2 h

slides.title: Lesson outline
bullets: Textbook material: Internal quality control: three phases; Control materials and rules for using them; Sources of error in the analytical phase and how to remove them; Pre-analytical factors and final control
Reference values: Reference values and decision limits
Practice: Q&A: 6 + 3

slides.title: Internal quality control: three phases
bullets: Internal quality control of laboratory tests is carried out every day, in every analytical series.
It covers all stages of testing — from preparing the patient to using the results: the pre-analytical, analytical and final (post-analytical) phases.
Pre-analytical phase: preparing the patient, collecting the material, registration, primary processing of the sample, delivery to the laboratory and storage until analysis.
Analytical phase: correct choice of method, correct dosing of material and reagents, setting up the reaction, measuring and calculating the result.

Final phase: correct completion of forms, evaluation of results and the conditions under which they reach the treating physician; results are recorded in a special log and the correct entry of reference values is checked.

slides.title: Internal quality control: three phases
bullets: The basis of internal control is regular testing of a standardised control material and recording the results on a control chart.

slides.title: Control materials and rules for using them
bullets: For internal control, factory-made control materials approved for use in Uzbekistan are recommended; if they are unavailable, controls prepared from leftovers of unused samples (serum, plasma, urine) may be used.
For haematology: stabilised blood, special suspensions for checking cell counts, haemolysates and fixed blood smears.
For biochemistry, control sera: frozen, lyophilised (animal or human) and liquid human serum; they differ in similarity to patient samples, cost, stability, dilution error and infection risk.
Before use, read the manufacturer’s instructions (data sheet) carefully.
Even when the instructions say the material is free of hepatitis and HIV antigens, handle control material with great care.
When preparing it: open the vial carefully to avoid spills, measure the solvent exactly, mix without foaming once the cap is tightly closed, and respect the dissolving time.

slides.title: Sources of error in the analytical phase and how to remove them
bullets: General laboratory factors: contamination (check water purity and pH, the caps of reagent vials and the pipettes) and technical errors — work order, temperature, incubation time and dosing inaccuracies.
Reagents: expiry date, solvent volume and water quality, storage rules (storage above 37 °C strongly affects stability); a doubtful result is re-checked with fresh reagents.
Control material: reconstitution rules, pipette and water quality, stability; a doubtful result is checked with freshly prepared control.

Samples: quality of collection, centrifugation (speed and temperature), separating serum or plasma from cells as soon as possible, keeping containers closed and using plastic only; turbid, haemolysed, lipaemic and highly bilirubin-rich serum/plasma is not tested.

slides.title: Sources of error in the analytical phase and how to remove them
bullets: Instrument: if possible, re-check the result on another instrument; check calibration and program parameters; avoid scratched cuvettes; wipe the optics.
Errors also stem from low staff qualification, calculation mistakes and inaccuracies in reagent preparation.

slides.title: Pre-analytical factors and final control
bullets: Factors that influence the result: errors in registering the patient and the biomaterial; biological factors (sex, age, physiological state, biorhythms, diet and fasting, body position, physical activity, smoking, alcohol); iatrogenic factors (diagnostic procedures, operations, treatment, drugs).
Collection conditions matter too: time of collection, preparation of the body site, cleanliness of containers, primary processing (centrifugation), storage and dispatch to the laboratory.

Blood is recommended to be drawn in outpatients between 8 and 10 a.m., in inpatients after waking or between 7 and 9 a.m., fasting or after a light breakfast, lying or sitting; drawing after physiotherapy, X-ray or physical exertion is not recommended.
The most effective way to prevent errors outside the laboratory is to work together with clinicians.

slides.title: Pre-analytical factors and final control
bullets: Final control: check the analytical plausibility of the result and its match with the passport part of the referral, and compare it with earlier or parallel results of the same patient — a large difference is discussed with the physician and the test repeated if needed.
The time the result is sent is shown on the form: especially in urgent cases, holding results back can seriously affect the timeliness of care.

slides.title: Control material prepared from horse serum can be used in the following cases:
options: if additives are present
dissolves within 60 minutes
turbidity less than 0.2 units. Extinction (cuvette 0.3 cm; wavelength 630–690 nm)
yellow in color and lustrous

slides.title: Not used in quality control of coagulation tests:
options: Fresh pooled plasma from many donors (at least 20 people), standard lyophilized human plasma for calibration
plasma prepared from human plasma with a precise concentration of coagulation factors (normal and pathological)
control plasma deficient in some coagulation factors
Fresh plasma obtained from a donor

slides.title: Quality management method that does not require control materials:
options: Study of parallel samples, repeat testing of the sample
Use of constants
Average of normals method
All of the above

slides.title: Interlaboratory quality control makes it possible to:
options: Certify control materials
Compare the quality of work of several laboratories
Standardize the examination method
Assess the quality of the methods used

slides.title: It is proposed to use the following for quality control of biochemical tests:
options: aqueous solution of substrates
ready-made commercially produced serum (liquid or lyophilized)
donor blood
reagents of foreign companies

slides.title: A control chart is:
options: a set of tests from one day
a graphical plot of measurements depending on the time of examination
an accounting chart of control results
an accounting chart of results

slides.title: General rules for quality control of clinical laboratory tests?
bullets: 1. The quality assurance system covers the entire testing process (pre-pre → preanalytical → analytical → postanalytical → post-post); the standard is ISO 15189:2022.

2. Internal quality control: in each run (at least daily) control materials at two or more levels, Levey–Jennings charts and Westgard rules; if a run is not accepted, patient results are not released, the cause is found, corrected and recorded.
3. External quality assessment (interlaboratory comparison, PT) – regular participation, analysis of results and corrective actions.
4. Equipment and reagents: calibration, preventive maintenance, temperature control, checking reagent lots and expiry; method verification/validation.
5. Staff competence, SOPs, documentation and traceability; quality indicators (specimen rejection, turnaround time, critical value notifications) and internal audits.

slides.title: Quality of laboratory tests and the factors affecting it?
bullets: 1. The quality of a laboratory result is its fitness for a clinical decision: trueness (absence of systematic error), precision/repeatability (small random error), timely release, correct interpretation.
2. Preanalytical factors (more than half of errors): incorrect ordering, patient preparation, identification errors, wrong tube, hemolysis, clot, low volume, transport and storage.

3. Analytical factors: calibration, reagent quality and expiry, instrument malfunction, interferences (hemolysis, lipemia, bilirubin, drugs), staff qualification; detected by internal and external control.
4. Postanalytical factors: incorrect entry/transmission of the result, wrong unit or reference interval, failure to report a critical value, delay.
5. Biological factors: age, sex, circadian rhythm, pregnancy, diet, physical exertion – taken into account in reference intervals and interpretation.

slides.title: Principles of quality control of clinical laboratory tests?
bullets: 1. Basic principles: control applies to the entire testing process, is regular and documented, statistically based, and aimed at preventing and correcting errors (continuous improvement).
2. Control materials should have a matrix similar to the patient sample, concentrations close to clinical decision levels, and be independent of the calibrator.
3. Statistical control: the mean (x̄), standard deviation (SD) and coefficient of variation (CV%) are determined; acceptance/rejection of a run by the Levey–Jennings chart and Westgard multirules.
4. External control assesses trueness (bias); method performance is compared with quality requirements.
5. For each nonconformity – corrective and preventive actions, records and staff training (ISO 15189).
